meta.rule: A question is BLOCKING if a decision cannot be made without it. Where a question is blocking and unanswered, the site records the decision as pending and the dependent strategy stays at status 'blocked'. Nothing downstream is filled in with a guess.

legend.known: what is already established, with source
legend.default: the fallback if the reviewer never answers
legend.tier: T1 official / T2 trusted secondary / T3 unverified

groups.title: Market data and line origination inputs
groups.why_this_group_matters: The stated goal is to originate NFL lines. A line is a price; a price requires a market to price against. This repo currently has no market-data feed of any kind, which blocks every quantitative deliverable in the brief.

questions.question: Which source will supply pre-game and closing prices, and at what update frequency?
questions.known: No odds feed is reachable from this workspace: outbound network is restricted to github.com, npmjs.org and pypi.org, so no sportsbook or aggregator endpoint could be read here. Verified: the injury/standings layer is reachable through nfl.com and is captured; the price layer is absent.
questions.unknown: Vendor, licence cost, whether timestamped line *history* (not just current price) is available, and whether player-prop prices are included.
questions.resolve: Pick one of: a commercial odds API, an exchange (betfair-style) API, or a self-maintained scraper on licensed accounts. Ask each vendor for: (a) open/close/midnight snapshots, (b) prop coverage, (c) redistribution rights.
options: Manual sportsbook capture on a schedule
questions.default: Stay blocked. Publish model architecture only, with all price fields blank.

evidence.label: NFL official data hub (availability, injuries, standings) - confirmed reachable

questions.question: Do we treat one book as the 'sharpest anchor' (i.e. our proxy for market truth), and which?
questions.known: Strategy value depends on it: 'beat the close' only means something if 'the close' is a defined, liquid, low-limit-sensitive price.
questions.unknown: Which venue the reviewer considers efficient, and whether it accepts the reviewer's account type/limits.
questions.resolve: After the feed decision, compute for each book: median time-to-move after an availability news event, and median vig. The book that moves fastest and holds the tightest vig is the anchor. This is measurable, not opinion.
questions.default: Consensus of 3+ books, with per-book dispersion reported.

questions.question: Which markets are in scope: side, total, moneyline, team totals, first half, player props, alternates, live?
questions.known: The brief names single bets, parlays and player-prop combos, so spreads/totals/props are in scope at minimum.
questions.unknown: Whether prop and alternate lines have *historical* depth (they are thinner than sides/totals and often not archived), and whether live betting is allowed.
questions.resolve: Ask the data vendor for row counts per market per week for the last 3 seasons before committing to prop modelling.
questions.default: Side, total, moneyline, team totals. Props gated behind a data-availability check.

questions.question: What is the settlement/no-action rule set we model (voided props, postponements, OT, cancelled games)?
questions.known: Rules are operator-specific; a pipeline that assumes one rule set misprices parlays.
questions.unknown: The reviewer's operator(s) and their published rules.
questions.resolve: Store the operator rule text per market type in the repo and version it; the simulator reads it instead of assuming.
questions.default: Model operator rules exactly for live; 'ignore' allowed only in research mode and must be labelled.

groups.title: Bankroll, staking and execution
groups.why_this_group_matters: Every 'is this strategy good' question is unanswerable without a stake and cost model, because the same signal is either profitable or ruinous depending on sizing.

questions.question: What is the bankroll and the maximum number of units at risk per week and per game?
questions.known: Gates can bound risk only relative to a stated bankroll; Kelly fractions, ruin probability and drawdown limits are all meaningless without it.
questions.unknown: Bankroll size, currency, and whether it is money the reviewer can lose entirely.
questions.resolve: Reviewer states a number and a hard weekly stop-loss. Until then, the site runs in unit-based research mode with zero currency exposure.
questions.default: Research only. No stake size is computed and the site says so.

questions.question: What staking rule: flat, percentage, or fractional Kelly, and at what fraction?
questions.known: Full Kelly on an estimated edge over-bets, because the estimate's error is not in the formula. Fractional Kelly is the standard mitigation.
questions.unknown: The reviewer's risk tolerance and whether the edge estimate is treated as noisy (it should be).
questions.resolve: Fix by policy in config, then never tune it on the same data used to select strategies.
questions.default: 0.25x Kelly with a hard 1.5%-of-bankroll cap per bet.

questions.question: Who places the bets, and what is the allowed latency between signal and commitment?
questions.known: The brief requires no manual input from the reviewer. 'No manual input' from the reviewer does not mean no human in the loop for capital release.
questions.unknown: Whether the system may place orders autonomously, or must queue them for confirmation, and whether limits/locks make late bets unfillable.
questions.resolve: Define the execution contract: signal timestamp → order placed, in seconds; measure realised fill rate before a strategy is allowed live.
questions.default: Queue with auto-expiry; anything unfillable is logged as a miss, not skipped silently.

questions.question: Is there a hard responsible-gambling guardrail (budget cap, cool-off, no chase-bet rule) enforced in code?
questions.known: This project's stated purpose is wagering. A system that can size up after losses is the standard failure mode, and the failure is total, not statistical.
questions.unknown: The cap values and who may change them.
questions.resolve: Implement caps as an immutable config the optimiser cannot write to; require a separate manual key to raise them.
questions.default: Code-enforced caps, default-on, cannot be raised by any automated job.

groups.title: Legal, jurisdiction and data rights
groups.why_this_group_matters: Two separate legal surfaces: the act of betting, and the act of collecting the data. Both are unresolved and both can end the project.

questions.question: Which jurisdiction will place wagers, and is that jurisdiction's licensing status confirmed for the chosen operator?
questions.known: The reviewer's session context is Mexico City, Mexico. This is an environment observation, not a legal finding, and no legal advice is offered here.
questions.unknown: Whether the intended operator is licensed where the reviewer is, and what the local rules on offshore/online wagering are.
questions.resolve: A single licensed-operator check plus one counsel confirmation before any capital is exposed. This is the cheapest question in the project to answer and the most expensive to ignore.
questions.default: Research only. No operator integration.

questions.question: Do the data licences permit storing, transforming and republishing what we derive from them (this site publishes tables)?
questions.known: The site is public. League data pages are the source for the injury/standings tables; vendor terms govern any price data added later.
questions.unknown: Redistribution terms of the eventual odds vendor, and whether automated retrieval of club/league pages is permitted under their published terms.
questions.resolve: Keep a per-source terms note in data/signals/sources.json and restrict the public site to aggregate facts, not scraped verbatim payloads.
questions.default: Facts and aggregates only; each row keeps an attribution link.

questions.question: Does the leaderboard reward real money, and if so does a reward pool that depends on wagering results create a promotion/eligibility problem?
questions.known: Brief asks for 'rewards for top performing strategies'. Reward design is a governance choice, not a technical one.
questions.unknown: Who may receive rewards, whether non-employees compete, and tax treatment.
questions.resolve: Default to non-cash 'research credit' rewards (compute hours, data spend, capital allocation priority) which sidesteps most of the question.
questions.default: Non-cash credits; capital allocation priority is the only real-money consequence.

groups.title: Model and evaluation policy
groups.why_this_group_matters: 'Remove luck from the equation' is a specification, and specifications need numbers attached to them before code can enforce them.

questions.question: Is a strategy judged on realised PnL or on closing-line value (CLV)?
questions.known: PnL needs thousands of bets before luck washes out; CLV is measurable on every bet the next day and is the standard early signal of edge. The brief explicitly asks to remove luck, which points at CLV.
questions.unknown: Whether the reviewer accepts a leaderboard that can rank a strategy highly before it has made money.
questions.resolve: Adopt CLV as primary, PnL as confirmation, and say it on the leaderboard so nobody misreads a rank as proof.
questions.default: CLV primary for promotion decisions; PnL displayed but marked 'not yet significant'.

questions.question: What minimum sample and significance level does a strategy need before it can move up a tier?
questions.known: Without a pre-registered n and alpha, the leaderboard selects noise - the single most common way a 'skill-based' system is actually a variance lottery.
questions.unknown: The reviewer's tolerance for waiting (more bets = slower promotion).
questions.resolve: Adopt the gate defaults in /validation.html (500 bets and a Bonferroni-adjusted test across all variants tried) and change only by written decision.
questions.default: 500 bets, alpha 0.05 after correction for the number of variants tried.

questions.question: Which ground-truth strength metric does the model predict before it predicts prices: points, EPA, or a blend?
questions.known: Origination is easier to validate if it predicts a team-strength state that is measured independently of the scoreboard.
questions.unknown: Whether a per-play expected-points feed is licensed for use here.
questions.resolve: Availability check against the league's public stats surface and any purchased provider; else fall back to points-differential state.
questions.default: Points differential with opponent adjustment (fully computable from verified box scores).

evidence.label: League stats surface (availability to be confirmed for automated retrieval)

questions.question: How are historical injury reports assembled for backtesting, given only the current week is served on the public report page?
questions.known: The public report page exposes a season and week selector, which implies the league retains prior weeks; only the selected week is rendered. No historical archive is present in this repo today.
questions.unknown: Whether every past week is retrievable for the seasons we need, and at what completeness (the page shows only players a club chose to list).
questions.resolve: Snapshot every weekly report into the repo immediately (append-only, dated), so history accumulates from now on; separately test whether older weeks resolve through the same selector.
questions.default: Accumulate now; treat any pre-snapshot season as unavailable and mark backtests that claim it as invalid.

evidence.label: Week/season selector on the official report page

questions.question: What is the correlation policy for parlay pricing: assumed independence, a capped adjustment, or a fully modelled joint distribution?
questions.known: Assuming independence in a same-game parlay systematically overprices correlated legs, which is precisely where books make their margin. The brief asks for correlation values to be determined.
questions.unknown: Measured joint-settlement rates per leg-pair in this environment; no bet ledger exists yet to measure them from.
questions.resolve: Estimate empirically from settled same-game legs (see /correlation.html protocol) and refuse to price any parlay whose leg-pair has fewer than the minimum observations.
questions.default: Refuse to price any pair with no measured correlation; publish the blank.

questions.question: Which 'luck removal' diagnostic is authoritative when CLV and PnL disagree?
questions.known: They will disagree. A strategy can beat the close and still lose for 300 bets; a strategy can win money while consistently losing to the close, which is the dangerous case.
questions.unknown: The tie-break rule the reviewer wants the leaderboard to apply.
questions.resolve: Pre-register: CLV positive and PnL negative = 'keep, under review'; CLV negative and PnL positive = 'kill'. Record the rule so the decision is not made after seeing the money.
questions.default: CLV wins for retention, PnL wins for capital allocation.

groups.title: Availability, depth and the backup-replacement problem
groups.why_this_group_matters: The brief's core data ask - 'know when 2nd/3rd/4th-string backups replace starters' - is exactly the part the official weekly report does NOT contain. It states who is unavailable, not who replaces them or how much quality that costs.

questions.question: What is the authoritative depth-chart source, and does it update in time for Friday pricing?
questions.known: Verified from the official report: it lists player, position, practice participation and game status - and nothing about the replacement. So 'backup replaces starter' must come from a separate feed.
questions.unknown: Whether each club publishes a machine-readable, timestamped depth chart on its official site, and how often it is stale.
questions.resolve: Pick one: club-official depth charts (T1 but 32 formats), a trusted aggregation, or derive our own line-ups from played-snap data after the fact (accurate, but only for backtests).
options: Derive from snaps after the game (backtest-only)
questions.default: Derive for research; do not originate live prices from depth assumptions.

evidence.label: Official Week 10 report - schema confirmed, no depth field

questions.question: How do we value a replacement: named-player skill, a position-decay ladder, or 'starters lost' counts?
questions.known: Counting absent players (the naive approach) treats losing a starting centre as losing a starting cornerback. It is wrong in a way that biases specific markets.
questions.unknown: Any per-position replacement-value curve validated on NFL data - none exists in this repo, and none was verified from an official source in this session.
questions.resolve: Estimate empirically: regress achieved team performance on the availability-weighted quality of the affected position group. Requires the snap/usage feed from Q-ROSTER-03.
options: Player-level value from a licensed metric
questions.default: Position ladder, with every coefficient marked 'estimated, unvalidated' until the regression runs.

questions.question: Is per-play tracking / snap-count data licensed for use?
questions.known: Usage reallocation after an absence is where prop edge lives; without snaps and targets the prop model can only use priors, which is guesswork with extra steps.
questions.unknown: Licensing and cost for tracking/next-gen data in this project.
questions.resolve: Confirm against the league's data licensing surface before committing to any prop strategy; otherwise descope props.
questions.default: Box-score aggregates only; prop combos stay in research tier.

evidence.label: League next-gen stats product (licensing terms not read in this session)

questions.question: Do we ingest transactions (IR, practice-squad elevations, waiver claims) as a separate feed from the weekly report?
questions.known: Verified in the Week 10 snapshot: the league news column reported a quarterback placed on injured reserve with a replacement 'in line for first start'. That is an IR move - it changes who the backups are for weeks, yet the weekly report only shows a game-status line. Also confirmed in the same snapshot: a mid-season trade changed a player's club, so any season-long roster prior is stale by design.
questions.unknown: The exact machine-readable transactions endpoint and its update cadence.
questions.resolve: Add a transactions snapshot job alongside the injury job; treat a missing transaction row as a data gap, not as 'nothing happened'.
questions.default: Yes, daily snapshot; flag any week where the two feeds disagree.

evidence.label: League report page: IR move and trade visible in the news column beside the report

questions.question: How is a 'confirmed starter' distinguished from 'expected to start', and does a model ever act on the unconfirmed one?
questions.known: Verified in the Week 10 snapshot: headlines used 'no designation, will start', 'expected to start again', and 'in line for first start' - three different confidence levels. One row in the captured report (a Rams wide receiver) shows 'likely to be placed on injured reserve' in the headline while the report itself lists no game status, which is a direct example of headline and report disagreeing.
questions.unknown: A machine-usable confidence label for line-up news - none exists in the source data.
questions.resolve: Attach our own label from the source sentence ('ruled out' / 'confirmed' / 'expected' / 'report:'), and forbid pricing off 'report:' items.
options: Pricing on expected with a haircut
Never price news, only the report
questions.default: Price only confirmed designations; 'expected' moves the model's variance, not its mean.

evidence.label: Headline: 'likely' IR placement, no game status on report

groups.title: Governance of this project and this site
groups.why_this_group_matters: The brief asks for a place to review suggestions and choose a path, and simultaneously asks for no manual input. Those pull in opposite directions; the split has to be decided, not assumed.

questions.question: What is automated without review, what is automated but reversible, and what needs a human yes?
questions.known: The brief says 'no manual input on my part' for producing work, and separately says suggestions must be reviewed before changes are implemented.
questions.unknown: The boundary line. Reasonable default: all research, capture, modelling and publishing is automated; anything that releases capital, changes a gate threshold, or deletes history needs a decision.
questions.resolve: Adopt or amend the default split in /suggestions.html (status field is the control).
questions.default: Default split.

questions.question: Who is the reviewer that changes a suggestion from 'proposed' to 'approved' or 'rejected', and does silence mean approval?
questions.known: Silence-as-approval is how unexamined systems end up implementing the worst suggestion by default.
questions.unknown: The named reviewer and any timeout policy.
questions.resolve: Name one reviewer; make the default 'stays proposed forever' rather than 'auto-approved'.
questions.default: Explicit approval required for anything irreversible.

questions.question: Does the leaderboard get its own capital budget, or does it only rank research?
questions.known: A leaderboard that allocates money creates incentive to overfit and to farm sample size; gates mitigate but do not remove this.
questions.unknown: Whether the reviewer wants allocation consequences tied to rank, and at what cap.
questions.resolve: Start with rank affecting only 'priority for capital review', never automatic sizing.
questions.default: Rank sets priority order for a human allocation review; it never moves money by itself.

questions.question: How are unverified rows meant to be resolved - by a human, or by a follow-up session with better access?
questions.known: This build never fills a cell it could not read; blanks plus a flagged row is the enforced behaviour, and every blank is listed on /flagged.html with the reason.
questions.unknown: Whether the reviewer wants an agent session with network access to a market-data vendor, or will supply an export.
questions.resolve: Either grant a network-accessible environment for the ingestion job, or drop a CSV export into /data/inbox/; the builder treats both identically.
questions.default: Leave blank; keep on the flagged page.
